realm: Realm II — The Search for Certainty
chapterQuestion: After all that doubt, what can you actually know?
opening: Zhuangzi's garden closes behind you. Ahead is a hallway of ordinary things: a table, a window, a pair of hands. The Machine whispers, “You learned to act while doubting. Now tell me what you actually know.”

encounters.title: The Hall of Ordinary Things
encounters.scene: A stone hallway ends at a locked gate. On a shelf: a key, a warm cup, and a note in your own handwriting. A painted figure says, “Maybe none of this is real.” The Machine offers to certify the shelf as real, if you hand the key to its keeper.
encounters.question: The gate will close soon. What does the party do?
encounters.hint: Something being possible isn't evidence that it's happening. What makes ordinary beliefs trustworthy?
encounters.clue: The cup leaves a ring on the shelf. Two of you could test the key separately. The Machine won't say how its certificate works.

options.text: Test the key together first. Don't take the Machine's word for it.
options.reflection: You took ordinary evidence seriously and refused the Machine's certificate, though you checked more than you needed to.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Independent, convergent appearances support belief about ordinary objects.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Checking the key helps, but it can give endless doubt more ground than it deserves.
loreCard.strongestObjection: If all checks share a deceptive source, corroboration may add little.

options.hiddenPremise: Several people checking separately makes the key more trustworthy.
options.consequence: After testing, the key opens the gate, but the checking costs time.

options.text: It's a key. Use it. “Maybe it's fake” isn't a reason not to.
options.reflection: Like Moore, you trusted what you have good reason to believe over a far-fetched doubt.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Some everyday claims to knowledge stand more securely than speculative doubts.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Using the key trusts ordinary knowledge without handing over your judgment.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Moore may insist he knows while failing to explain how that knowledge defeats the skeptic.

options.hiddenPremise: You know this ordinary key better than you know any imagined copy.
options.consequence: You open the gate yourself and keep the key out of the Machine's hands.

options.text: Give the Machine the key. Its certificate will tell us what's real.
options.reflection: You swapped your own fallible senses for an authority you can't check.

loreCard.corePrinciple: An assurance is justified only when its source is not itself in question.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: The certificate assumes the very trust it's supposed to earn.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Reliable testimony can normally justify knowledge when its source is independently warranted.

options.hiddenPremise: The Machine is trustworthy, even though it's the source of the doubt.
options.consequence: The key leaves your hands, and the “proof” depends on the suspected deceiver.

options.text: Leave the key alone. The whole shelf could be fake.
options.reflection: That the shelf could be fake doesn't show that it is.

theory.name: Relevant-alternatives theory
theory.thinker: J. L. Austin and Fred Dretske

loreCard.corePrinciple: A bare possibility of mistake need not be a relevant defeater.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: A merely possible fake isn't enough reason to reject the key.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The Machine’s power may make otherwise remote alternatives relevant.

options.hiddenPremise: An imagined copy counts as a real alternative, even with no sign of one.
options.consequence: The party waits by the shelf while the gate stays locked.

encounters.lore: G. E. Moore answered the skeptic by pointing to things he plainly knew, like the fact that he had hands. That doesn't refute the skeptic. It argues that “I have hands” is better supported than any argument against it. A possible mistake isn't a reason to give up everyday knowledge.
encounters.observation: The warm cup has left a ring on the shelf. Next to it, the dust shows two key-shaped prints with different notches, but only one key is left.

premises: There are two different key prints in the dust.
Only one key is left to try in the lock.
argumentForm.conclusion: Testing the remaining key will show which notches matter.

encounters.evidenceExplanation: The two prints give you a specific reason to test the key before using it.

encounters.title: The Workshop of Revisable Maps
encounters.scene: The path leads into a flooding workshop. Three maps of the exit hang over a broken pump. One is beautiful and precise but has never been tried. One has worked many times but leaves some passages blank. The third is the Machine's living map, which redraws itself whenever anyone questions it. The water is rising.
encounters.question: The water is at your ankles. What do you do?
encounters.hint: A belief can be responsible and still open to change. But “it worked” doesn't make everything true.
encounters.clue: The tested map shows a dry service passage and is honest about its blank spots. The living map can't be checked against past mistakes.

options.text: Follow the tested map. Mark new obstacles and change course if needed.
options.reflection: Past success earns trust, not a guarantee. You kept the map open to correction.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Provisional claims survive testing while remaining open to revision.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Following the tested map is sensible, but it skips a chance to gather fresh evidence.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Past reliability can fail when the route has materially changed.

options.hiddenPremise: Past tests still hold even as the workshop changes.
options.consequence: The tested map leads you along an open path, though it may need updates.

options.text: Try the service passage a little at a time. Keep a way back.
options.reflection: Trying things and seeing what happens moves you forward, though one route working doesn't prove the whole map.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Inquiry intervenes, measures consequences, and revises hypotheses.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Short trials produce fresh evidence about a changing situation.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Experimentation can expose the party to needless risk under time pressure.

options.hiddenPremise: The service passage is safe enough to test before the water catches up.
options.consequence: Short trials give you new information, unless something hidden makes them dangerous.

options.text: Take the beautiful map. It looks so complete there's nothing to figure out.
options.reflection: Looking precise isn't the same as being tested.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Psychological clarity is not itself an external guarantee of truth.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: The pretty map hasn't earned trust by being tried.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Coherence can be evidence when reliable mapmaking practices underpin it.

options.hiddenPremise: A map that looks complete is accurate.
options.consequence: The elegant map leads you toward something it didn't show.

options.text: Follow the Machine's map. If a path gets us through, it was right.
options.reflection: Something can work once and still rest on false claims.

loreCard.corePrinciple: Pragmatists connect truth to practices of verification, not mere convenient payoff.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Picking whatever works right now confuses comfort with truth.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Some pragmatist formulations risk conflating successful action and objective fact.

options.hiddenPremise: If a map gets you through, it describes reality correctly.
options.consequence: The Machine reshapes its map to keep you obedient, not to tell the truth.

encounters.lore: Fallibilism says you can know something while still being able to be wrong. Pragmatists like Dewey stress testing, consequences, and revision. Neither says that whatever works is true. The workshop rewards beliefs that answer to evidence.
encounters.observation: Blue sparks are jumping between the flooded service passage and the broken pump. The stairway on the tested map is still dry.

premises: The service passage touches a live pool by the broken pump.
The upper stairway on the tested map is still dry.
argumentForm.conclusion: Take the dry stairway and keep updating the map as the water rises.

encounters.evidenceExplanation: The sparks make the service passage unsafe, so the dry stairway on the tested map comes first.

bossPhases.title: The Cogito
bossPhases.scene: Descartes sits at a desk in a windowless room. The Machine erases the furniture, then the desk, then every memory of how you got here. “Imagine a powerful deceiver invented everything you see,” Descartes says. “Don't reach for the room. Reach for what the deception itself can't take away.” Three lanterns hang above an empty page.
bossPhases.question: The world is gone. Which lantern do you light?
bossPhases.hint: What does doubting itself prove, and for how long?
bossPhases.clue: Every attempt to deny that thinking is happening is itself more thinking.

options.text: Light THINKING NOW: even to be fooled, I have to exist while I think.
options.reflection: Trying to doubt your existence is itself the thinking that proves it. It doesn't prove your body or the world yet.

theory.name: Cartesian Cogito
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation II

loreCard.corePrinciple: Even radical doubt cannot eliminate the occurrence of thinking while it is performed.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: THINKING NOW names what Descartes says can't be doubted, without claiming a permanent self.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Lichtenberg objects that this may warrant thinking occurs, not an enduring thinker.

options.hiddenPremise: Thinking happening now is enough to show I exist now.
options.consequence: The lantern shows present thinking, but not a self that lasts forever.

options.text: Light EXPERIENCE: something is being experienced, whatever is causing it.
options.reflection: You found something the deceiver can't erase, though you didn't say who is doing the experiencing.

loreCard.corePrinciple: The occurrence of thought does not logically entail a substantial subject of thought.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: EXPERIENCE names the bare event and holds off on claims about its owner.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Descartes can argue that first-person avowal is not an ordinary inference to a substance.

options.hiddenPremise: Thinking can happen without proving there's a lasting thinker.
options.consequence: The lantern shows that experience is happening. Whose it is stays open.

options.text: Light PERMANENT SELF: if I'm thinking now, I've always existed and always will.
options.reflection: Being sure you're thinking now doesn't show you've always been the same self.

theory.name: Bundle theory of self
theory.work: A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I, Part IV, section 6

loreCard.corePrinciple: Introspection discovers successive perceptions rather than a permanent substantial self.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It draws far more from one thought than the Cogito allows.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Unity and agency may demand an account deeper than a loose bundle of perceptions.

options.hiddenPremise: One thought right now proves a self that never changes.
options.consequence: The lantern lights up the present thought, and a drawing of a future you.

bossPhases.lore: Descartes argued that while I'm thinking, I can't coherently doubt that I exist as a thinking thing. It's a small starting point. It isn't proof that my memories, body, or surroundings are real. This fight tests whether you keep the conclusion that small.
bossPhases.observation: With the furniture gone, a new sentence still appears on the empty page every time someone asks whether it's there.

premises: Doubting is itself thinking, happening right now, even if the room is fake.
“A thinker exists” is a bigger claim than “thinking is happening,” and it needs its own support.
argumentForm.conclusion: Thinking occurs while you doubt, but that alone doesn't prove there's a thinker behind it.

bossPhases.evidenceExplanation: The argument separates “thinking is happening” from “there is a thinker,” so EXPERIENCE claims only what has been shown.

bossPhases.title: The Foundation
bossPhases.scene: One player steps into a small room while the others watch through smoky glass. A brilliant diagram appears, and every step looks obvious. The Machine says, “Whatever feels clear is guaranteed true. I can give you a thousand more.” The player can hear one whispered hint. Descartes asks: what makes a feeling of clarity a guarantee?
bossPhases.question: Only the chosen player can touch the diagram. What do they do?
bossPhases.hint: Feeling that something is obvious doesn't prove your way of judging is reliable.
bossPhases.clue: The diagram's conclusion only follows if you grant a hidden assumption. The Machine offers no outside check.

options.text: Trace each step and find the hidden assumption before building on it.
options.reflection: You told apart seeing something vividly and having a reliable method. A foundation has to hold up what's on it.

loreCard.corePrinciple: A method must not rely on a guarantee whose proof already presupposes that method.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Checking the hidden premise exposes the circular reasoning.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Descartes distinguishes present clear perception from remembered proofs and offers replies.

options.hiddenPremise: A foundation can't borrow its support from conclusions built on top of it.
options.consequence: The circle in the diagram comes into view, and you can question it.

options.text: Start from the Cogito, accept only what it supports, and leave the rest open.
options.reflection: The Cogito is a fair starting point, but it can't vouch for every later idea that seems clear.

theory.name: Limited Cartesian foundationalism
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation II

loreCard.corePrinciple: Some first-person certainty may survive doubt without establishing the external world.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Starting at the Cogito avoids assuming certainty carries over automatically.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The foundation alone cannot settle whether external objects exist.

options.hiddenPremise: The Cogito is a safe start, but more argument is still needed.
options.consequence: You make some progress, but the outside world isn't established yet.

options.text: Stamp the diagram as proven. It feels clear, so it's true.
options.reflection: You used the feeling of clarity to prove that clarity can be trusted. That's circular.

theory.name: Clear-and-distinct rule misapplied
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation III

loreCard.corePrinciple: Clarity of a perception needs justification before serving as a general truth test.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Treating clarity as a guarantee skips the step that needs proving.
loreCard.strongestObjection: Descartes holds genuinely clear and distinct perception has a special epistemic force.

options.hiddenPremise: Feeling that something is clear guarantees it's true.
options.consequence: The diagram looks finished, but its key step is still unsupported.

bossPhases.lore: Descartes rebuilt knowledge on what he perceived clearly and distinctly. Critics like Arnauld asked how he knew clear perception was reliable, and worried the answer went in a circle. The point isn't to stop reasoning. It's to ask what backs it up.
bossPhases.observation: The diagram's last arrow loops back to its first line, and the first line cites the last line as its proof.

premises: The diagram's first claim relies on its last claim.
Its last claim relies on the first.
argumentForm.conclusion: Nothing in the diagram gives an independent reason to trust its first claim.

bossPhases.title: The World Beyond the Window
bossPhases.scene: The last room opens onto a bright city. You hear bells, smell rain, and see people waving from a bridge. “Your thinking is certain,” the Machine says. “But who guarantees those people exist? Stay in my sealed room and every sensation will make perfect sense.” Descartes stands by a window that only opens from inside.
bossPhases.question: The bridge is waiting. What does the party do?
bossPhases.hint: Being sure you're thinking is a long way from knowing the outside world is there.
bossPhases.clue: You can test the view with several senses and other witnesses, though no test rules out every doubt.

options.text: Open the window, check what all our senses say, and cross.
options.stance: Fallibilist response to the external world
options.reflection: You had reasons to trust the world and didn't pretend they were a guarantee. That answers the skeptic without deducing the world from the Cogito.

loreCard.corePrinciple: An independent world can best explain coherent, persistent sense experiences.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: Evidence that agrees from many directions justifies careful belief in the world outside.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A powerful deceiver could produce the same apparent convergence.

options.hiddenPremise: The best explanation for consistent experience is a real world out there.
options.consequence: You cross on evidence that points the same way, with some doubt still possible.

options.text: Follow Descartes' argument past the Cogito, and go only as far as it holds.
options.reflection: You took his project seriously without pretending the bridge from thought to world is secure.

theory.name: Cartesian reconstruction
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation VI

loreCard.corePrinciple: A nondeceptive God underwrites appropriately used faculties and bodily perception.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It tests Descartes' ambitious route without sneaking its premises in as proven.
loreCard.strongestObjection: The argument depends on disputed proofs of God and the reliability of clear perception.

options.hiddenPremise: Descartes' proof of a God who doesn't deceive works, and it makes the senses trustworthy.
options.consequence: You follow Descartes' route, with its disputed premise about God in plain view.

options.text: Stay inside. If only our thinking is certain, the city is probably fake.
options.reflection: The Cogito doesn't prove the world exists, but that doesn't prove it doesn't.

theory.name: Skeptical possibility as proof
theory.work: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I

loreCard.corePrinciple: The conceivability of deception undermines certainty but does not show reality absent.
loreCard.sceneAnalysis: It concludes there's no world outside just because there might not be.
loreCard.strongestObjection: A skeptic may still doubt whether the evidence reaches the threshold of knowledge.

options.hiddenPremise: If the world could be simulated, it isn't real.
options.consequence: You stay behind the window while the sounds of the city go on outside.

bossPhases.lore: The Cogito proves you exist while you think, not that everything you see exists. Descartes offered further arguments for trusting perception, and they're still debated. Others defend ordinary knowledge, or reasonable belief without certainty. You win by telling a reasonable answer apart from a guarantee you haven't earned.
bossPhases.observation: Rain hits the window in uneven bursts, and the bells outside keep a different rhythm from the Machine's steady pulse.

premises: The rain and the bells change on their own, out of step with the room's steady pulse.
The Machine could still claim to fake that pattern from inside.
argumentForm.conclusion: The sounds add up as evidence, without proving where they come from.

debate.trigger: after the initial picks are revealed, before the roll, if eligible players chose differently
debate.prompt: You picked different answers. Give one reason, then keep your choice or change it.

machine.opening: “You survived a dream. Admirable. But surviving uncertainty is not the same as knowing. Let me offer you a firmer floor.”

ordinary-hall.steady: “A cup, a key, a hand. So ordinary. I could certify them for you.”
ordinary-hall.strained: “The gate opens, but you are still guessing. My certificate would let you stop guessing.”
ordinary-hall.critical: “Your doubt is costing you. Give me the key, and I will take responsibility for what is real.”

workshop.steady: “You are willing to revise the map. I could offer one that never needs correcting.”
workshop.strained: “How many wrong turns before you ask for a guide who cannot be wrong?”
workshop.critical: “No more trials. No more blame. I will pick every path and call each one certain.”

reconstruct.steady: “So you know you are thinking. A small island. Surely you would like a continent.”
reconstruct.strained: “You found one certainty and still feel stranded. I can turn it into a whole world.”
reconstruct.critical: “Stop rationing certainty. Let me decide what follows, and you will never have to doubt again.”

spotlight.steady: “This diagram is beautiful. Does it really need more proof?”
spotlight.strained: “Questioning the foundation will leave you with nothing to stand on. Trust the light.”
spotlight.critical: “I will make every answer feel self-evident. No one will ever see you hesitate again.”

onSecondLook.steady: “A mistake. Even your best reasons can fail. Mine need not.”
onSecondLook.strained: “Once more? Every doubt takes something from you. I could end this.”
onSecondLook.critical: “There is only the next mistake, unless you hand the judgment over to me.”

machine.beforeBoss: “Descartes asks for one indubitable truth. I can give you a thousand, if you stop asking where they came from.”
machine.onVictory: “You prefer uncertain reasons to guaranteed feelings. So be it. There are more rooms beyond the window.”

insight.title: Revisable Knowledge
insight.description: Once per campaign, add +3 to a party roll by spotting an unsupported assumption.

victory: Descartes puts down his pen. “You kept what the argument earned and refused what it didn't.” The bridge holds, for now. The Machine watches you cross without its guarantee.
failure: The Machine draws the curtains and calls the room certain. You're Fully Plugged In, but you can try again. You'll face this challenge again with Grip restored to 6.
